Vision-Language-Delta-Action: Learning Compact Deltas as Actionable Transition Interfaces for Robotic Manipulation

Lingsen Zhang1,2,∗  Wei Li1,2,∗  Jie He1,2  Henghua Zhang2

Kai Mo2  Shiyong Li2  Yanpeng Wang2  Rui Shao1,3,†

∗Equal Contribution  †Corresponding Author

1Harbin Institute of Technology, Shenzhen  2Baidu, Inc.  3Shenzhen Loop Area Institute

1  Introduction

Similar to human actions, robotic manipulation is a process of controlled physical state transformation [56, 49]. As shown in Fig. 1 (top), conditioned on visual observations, a robot must not only recognize the current scene and interpret the task-relevant physical context around it [27, 23], but also determine which part of the scene should change and how such change can be realized through continuous action execution [43, 1]. This requirement fundamentally distinguishes robotic manipulation from generic vision-language understanding, as the critical decision variable is not the complete visual state itself, but the task-relevant transition that drives the current state toward the desired physical outcome.

However, existing VLA and WAM paradigms share a common limitation in lacking a dedicated, action-grounded representation of task-relevant physical transitions. 1) Most VLA models still follow an observation-to-action formulation that entangles task-relevant object identification [26, 4, 53, 61], desired physical state-change inference, and executable action-chunk generation within a single policy. Without dedicated modeling of task-relevant state changes, the policy must implicitly infer the intended physical transition from action supervision alone, leaving a substantial representational gap between semantic understanding and action execution.

A straightforward way to bridge semantic understanding and action execution is future modeling, as illustrated in Fig. 1 (a) and (b). 2) WAMs predict future observations [59, 7, 54], visual latents [44, 39], or action-conditioned dynamics [2, 25] to provide temporal cues beyond the current observation. However, they typically represent the future as another complete state, causing task-relevant transition cues to remain entangled with static scene content and action-irrelevant variations. Moreover, future prediction is often used only as an auxiliary objective, without providing a structured intermediate variable that can directly guide action generation. Robotic manipulation instead requires a compact transition variable that captures task-relevant manipulation-centric changes, remains consistent with the overall direction of future evolution, and is directly grounded in executable actions.

Taken together, these limitations motivate a transition interface that is selective, predictive, and actionable. It should isolate task-relevant manipulation-centric changes, remain consistent with future evolution, and be directly consumable by the action generator. To this end, we propose Vision-Language-Delta-Action (VLDA), a new paradigm that models actionable transitions through a low-dimensional Delta interface rather than predicting the complete future state.

Specifically, VLDA instantiates the transition interface as a compact low-dimensional Delta that captures the task-relevant transition implied by the task. To make Delta both selective and predictive, VLDA introduces a unified learning objective with two complementary constraints. 1) Local Transition Filter (LT-Filter) distills sparse, manipulation-centric transition evidence from dense current-to-future visual differences, suppressing static scene content and action-irrelevant variations. 2) Global Transition Anchor (GT-Anchor) regularizes Delta with a coarse summary of future evolution, preventing overly local transition modeling and preserving the global direction of state change. Together, these constraints reconcile local transition selectivity with global predictive consistency, yielding a compact and future-grounded representation of task-relevant physical change. To make Delta directly actionable, VLDA further introduces 3) Delta-Driven Action Refinement (DDAR), which grounds Delta in the action manifold through Delta-action alignment and injects it into the action flow as a structured transition seed. The action expert then refines this transition-informed seed into executable action chunks conditioned on the predicted transition. Rather than treating future prediction as auxiliary supervision, VLDA therefore establishes a closed understanding-transition-execution loop, where vision-language representations interpret the task context, Delta specifies the required state transition, and DDAR realizes that transition through continuous action generation.

We evaluate VLDA on standard robotic manipulation benchmarks and challenging long-horizon tasks. Experimental results show that VLDA improves long-horizon consistency, robustness under distribution shifts, and generalization to complex manipulation scenarios. These results demonstrate that modeling actionable Delta provides a more effective alternative to both direct observation-to-action learning and full future-state prediction. Our contributions are summarized as follows:

  • •

    We introduce Vision-Language-Delta-Action (VLDA), a new robotic manipulation paradigm that replaces complete future-state prediction with a compact Delta serving as an actionable transition interface.

  • •

    We design a unified Delta learning objective with Local Transition Filter and Global Transition Anchor, enabling Delta to capture sparse task-relevant changes while remaining consistent with future transition trends.

  • •

    We develop Delta-Driven Action Refinement, which aligns Delta with the action manifold and uses it as a structured seed for action denoising, forming an explicit understanding-transition-execution loop.

2  Related Work

Observation-to-Action Learning in VLA Models.

Existing VLA models primarily employ action-token prediction, implemented either autoregressively or in parallel [5, 26, 27, 20, 41, 32], and continuous action experts based on diffusion or flow matching [11, 4, 23, 51, 33, 17, 34]. Despite different action decoders, both paradigms directly supervise actions from observations, requiring a single policy to jointly resolve task grounding, intended physical change, and motor realization. This creates a substantial gap between high-level semantic observations and low-level executable actions. VLDA bridges this gap with a compact Delta that explicitly mediates what should change and how that change is executed.

Predictive World-Action Modeling.

Recent WAMs couple future modeling with robot control through cascaded future-to-action generation [47, 30, 62], joint world-action prediction [16, 7, 54, 63], and predictive latent dynamics [18, 21, 40]. In these formulations, future prediction typically serves as an upstream context, a jointly decoded target, or a regularizer for action learning, with its contribution to control determined by architecture-specific fusion mechanisms. VLDA instead reparameterizes the prediction-control connection through a compact Delta, whose control role is explicitly defined by transition learning and Delta-driven action refinement.

Latent Action Representation Learning.

Discrete approaches tokenize visually inferred motion patterns for scalable VLA pretraining [52, 6, 9], while continuous formulations learn smooth latent control variables that can be mapped to embodiment-specific actions with limited supervision [35, 45]. CLAP [57] and LARA [37] further improve physical grounding by aligning visually inferred representations with robot actions or proprioceptive dynamics. However, these representations mainly serve as pseudo-action labels, pretraining targets, or shared control spaces. They do not explicitly isolate task-relevant physical changes under complementary local and global constraints, ground such changes in the action manifold, and use them to directly guide action refinement.

3  Preliminary & Problem Definition

Problem Definition.

We consider robotic manipulation at step tt, where the robot receives an instruction ll and observes st=(𝐈t,pt)s_{t}=(\mathbf{I}_{t},p_{t}). Here, 𝐈t={Itc}c=1C\mathbf{I}_{t}=\{I_{t}^{c}\}_{c=1}^{C} denotes multi-view RGB observations and ptp_{t} denotes proprioception. The policy predicts an action chunk 𝐀t=[at,…,at+H−1]∈ℝH×da\mathbf{A}_{t}=[a_{t},\ldots,a_{t+H-1}]\in\mathbb{R}^{H\times d_{a}}, where HH and dad_{a} denote the action horizon and dimension, respectively. During training, the corresponding future primary-camera image It+HpriI_{t+H}^{\mathrm{pri}} is available, while inference only relies on (st,l)(s_{t},l). Our objective is to exploit such training-time state evolution to improve p⁡(𝐀t∣st,l)p(\mathbf{A}_{t}\mid s_{t},l) without requiring future observations at deployment.

Conditional Flow Matching.

Given a clean target 𝐱0\mathbf{x}_{0} and source 𝐳\mathbf{z} under condition cc, both experts use the same linear conditional path and corresponding target velocity:

𝐱τ=(1−τ)​𝐱0+τ​𝐳,𝐮τ⋆=𝐳−𝐱0.\mathbf{x}_{\tau}=(1-\tau)\mathbf{x}_{0}+\tau\mathbf{z},\qquad\mathbf{u}_{\tau}^{\star}=\mathbf{z}-\mathbf{x}_{0}. (1)

The Action Expert uses the biased source 𝐳A=ϵA+γ​𝐛​(c)\mathbf{z}_{A}=\epsilon_{A}+\gamma\mathbf{b}(c) and directly predicts 𝐮^τ\hat{\mathbf{u}}_{\tau}. The World Expert uses 𝐳Δ=ϵΔ\mathbf{z}_{\Delta}=\epsilon_{\Delta} and xx-prediction, estimating 𝐱^0=fϑ​(𝐱τ,τ,c)\hat{\mathbf{x}}_{0}=f_{\vartheta}(\mathbf{x}_{\tau},\tau,c) and recovering velocity as

𝐮^τ=𝐱τ−𝐱^0τ,\hat{\mathbf{u}}_{\tau}=\frac{\mathbf{x}_{\tau}-\hat{\mathbf{x}}_{0}}{\tau}, (2)

where ϵA,ϵΔ∼𝒩⁡(0,I)\epsilon_{A},\epsilon_{\Delta}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I) denote the noise variables used by the Action and World Experts, respectively.

Exponential Moving Average.

EMA maintains a slowly evolving model copy to provide stable supervision targets. Let ψr\psi_{r} and ψ¯r\bar{\psi}_{r} denote the online and EMA weights at iteration rr, respectively. The EMA weights are recursively updated at every training iteration as

ψ¯r=m​ψ¯r−1+(1−m)​ψr,m∈[0,1),\bar{\psi}_{r}=m\bar{\psi}_{r-1}+(1-m)\psi_{r},~~m\in[0,1), (3)

where mm is the EMA momentum governing the temporal smoothing of teacher weights. The EMA model is not optimized by gradients and evolves smoothly during training.

4  Vision-Language-Delta-Action

4.1  Framework: Actionable Delta Modeling

Given the current state sts_{t} and language instruction ll, conventional VLA policies directly predict an action chunk 𝐀t\mathbf{A}_{t} as 𝐀t∼π(⋅∣st,l)\mathbf{A}_{t}\sim\pi(\cdot\mid s_{t},l). However, such a direct observation-to-action mapping requires a single policy to bridge high-level semantic understanding and low-level action execution within a unified end-to-end decision-making process, making long-horizon manipulation difficult to optimize.

To alleviate this burden, VLDA reformulates action generation as an understanding–transition–execution process. A VLM backbone first encodes the state-instruction pair into a multimodal context 𝐡t=ΦVLM​(st,l)\mathbf{h}_{t}=\Phi_{\mathrm{VLM}}(s_{t},l). VLDA then introduces a compact actionable Delta Δt\Delta_{t} as an intermediate transition variable that captures task-specified physical state changes. The action generation process is factorized as:

p⁡(𝐀t∣st,l)=∫pθ​(Δt∣𝐡t)​pϕ​(𝐀t∣𝐡t,Δt)​d​Δt.p(\mathbf{A}_{t}\mid s_{t},l)=\int p_{\theta}(\Delta_{t}\mid\mathbf{h}_{t})p_{\phi}(\mathbf{A}_{t}\mid\mathbf{h}_{t},\Delta_{t})\,\mathrm{d}\Delta_{t}. (4)

Here, pθp_{\theta} denotes the World Expert for transition prediction, while pϕp_{\phi} denotes the Action Expert for action generation conditioned jointly on both the inferred Delta and multimodal context.

Through this factorization, Delta serves as a compact transition interface between vision-language understanding and action generation, replacing redundant full future-state modeling with focused task-relevant state-change modeling for downstream action prediction in diverse robotic manipulation scenarios.

4.2  Actionable Transition Generation

As established in Equation (4), the World Expert pθp_{\theta} predicts the actionable Delta Δt\Delta_{t} from the multimodal context 𝐡t\mathbf{h}_{t}. We model pθp_{\theta} as a continuous-time flow-matching model in the Delta space, which generates a clean transition estimate Δ^t\hat{\Delta}_{t} while preserving the compact structure of the learned transition representation.

Inspired by the manifold perspective revisited in JiT [31], where natural data lies on a low-dimensional structured manifold while noise spans an unstructured high-dimensional space, we note that physical state changes in robotic manipulation are similarly constrained by scene geometry, kinematics, and object interactions rather than being arbitrarily distributed in the latent space. Thus, we adopt xx-prediction parameterization for transition generation. Given the noisy Delta state Δτ\Delta_{\tau} at flow time τ\tau, the model predicts

Δ^t=fθΔ​(Δτ,τ,𝐡t).\hat{\Delta}_{t}=f_{\theta}^{\Delta}(\Delta_{\tau},\tau,\mathbf{h}_{t}). (5)

The Δτ\Delta_{\tau} is introduced in Section 4.3, with its detailed construction deferred to the transition-learning objective below. Following the xx-prediction form, the corresponding velocity is analytically recovered as

𝐮^τΔ=Δτ−Δ^tτ.\hat{\mathbf{u}}_{\tau}^{\Delta}=\frac{\Delta_{\tau}-\hat{\Delta}_{t}}{\tau}. (6)

The predicted Δ^t\hat{\Delta}_{t} serves as a compact transition prior for action generation. To ensure that this prior captures task-relevant physical changes rather than collapsing into trivial representations, we introduce two complementary objectives: Local Transition Filter and Global Transition Anchor, which respectively emphasize selective local changes and coarse global consistency within the learned transition representation.

4.3  Local Transition Filter

Learning the transition prior for the World Expert necessitates a supervision target that isolates actionable physical changes from low-level visual redundancies for stable task-relevant transition learning. Instead of relying on raw pixels, we extract dense semantic features from the current and future observations:

𝐕t=Eon​(Itpri),𝐕¯t+H=Eema​(It+Hpri)∈ℝP×dv.\mathbf{V}_{t}=E_{\mathrm{on}}(I_{t}^{\mathrm{pri}}),~~\bar{\mathbf{V}}_{t+H}=E_{\mathrm{ema}}(I_{t+H}^{\mathrm{pri}})\in\mathbb{R}^{P\times d_{v}}. (7)

where PP denotes the number of spatial tokens. Specifically, EonE_{\mathrm{on}} and EemaE_{\mathrm{ema}} denote the two encoders, with comprehensive elaborations provided in Section 5. The dense transition is computed as 𝐃t=𝐕¯t+H−𝐕t.\mathbf{D}_{t}=\bar{\mathbf{V}}_{t+H}-\mathbf{V}_{t}.

Rather than reconstructing the entire future feature map, which contains substantial static redundancy, LT-Filter isolates the task-relevant dynamics by selecting the top-KK regions with the largest transition magnitudes, thereby focusing supervision on regions exhibiting the strongest transition evidence:

𝒦t\displaystyle\mathcal{K}_{t} =TopKK⁡({‖𝐃t,i‖2}i=1P),\displaystyle=\operatorname{TopK}_{K}\left(\{\|\mathbf{D}_{t,i}\|_{2}\}_{i=1}^{P}\right), (8)
Δt⋆\displaystyle\Delta_{t}^{\star} =g↓​(𝐃t,𝒦t)∈ℝK×dΔ.\displaystyle=g_{\downarrow}\left(\mathbf{D}_{t,\mathcal{K}_{t}}\right)\in\mathbb{R}^{K\times d_{\Delta}}.

Here, g↓g_{\downarrow} projects the selected transition tokens into a compact Delta space, with K≪PK\ll P and dΔ≪dvd_{\Delta}\ll d_{v}, which keeps the representation compact while retaining task-relevant transition evidence. We refer to Δt⋆\Delta_{t}^{\star} as the Delta target, which filters out static appearance information while retaining local changes that are most likely to be actionable. Given Δt⋆\Delta_{t}^{\star} and Gaussian noise ϵΔ∼𝒩⁡(0,I)\epsilon_{\Delta}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I), the Delta flow path is constructed as

Δτ=τ​ϵΔ+(1−τ)​Δt⋆,𝐮τΔ=ϵΔ−Δt⋆.\Delta_{\tau}=\tau\epsilon_{\Delta}+(1-\tau)\Delta_{t}^{\star},~~\mathbf{u}_{\tau}^{\Delta}=\epsilon_{\Delta}-\Delta_{t}^{\star}. (9)

Since the tokens indexed by 𝒦t\mathcal{K}_{t} form an unordered set, standard point-wise regression is permutation-sensitive. We therefore use an entropy-regularized transport plan to construct a balanced soft correspondence. For two token sets 𝐗,𝐘∈ℝK×d\mathbf{X},\mathbf{Y}\in\mathbb{R}^{K\times d}, we define the pairwise cost as

Ci​j=‖𝐱i−𝐲j‖22d.C_{ij}=\frac{\|\mathbf{x}_{i}-\mathbf{y}_{j}\|_{2}^{2}}{d}. (10)

To resolve the ambiguity caused by the unordered token structure, we formulate transition matching as a soft set-to-set assignment problem rather than enforcing fixed index-wise correspondence. The pairwise costs therefore characterize the compatibility between predicted and target transition tokens, while a balanced transport plan determines their soft correspondence in a permutation-invariant manner. The transport plan and set-matching loss are then jointly computed as follows:

𝐓η⋆\displaystyle\mathbf{T}_{\eta}^{\star} =Sinkhornη⁡(𝐂¯),\displaystyle=\operatorname{Sinkhorn}_{\eta}(\bar{\mathbf{C}}), (11)
𝒟set​(𝐗,𝐘,d)\displaystyle\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{set}}(\mathbf{X},\mathbf{Y};d) =⟨sg⁡(𝐓η⋆),𝐂⟩,\displaystyle=\left\langle\operatorname{sg}(\mathbf{T}_{\eta}^{\star}),\mathbf{C}\right\rangle,

where 𝐂¯\bar{\mathbf{C}} is the sample-wise normalized cost, sg\operatorname{sg} denotes stop-gradient, and η\eta controls the softness of the balanced transport plan. The Local Transition Filter objective is then

ℒLTF=𝔼τ,ϵΔ​[𝒟set​(𝐮^τΔ,𝐮τΔ,dΔ)].\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{LTF}}=\mathbb{E}_{\tau,\epsilon_{\Delta}}\left[\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{set}}\left(\hat{\mathbf{u}}_{\tau}^{\Delta},\mathbf{u}_{\tau}^{\Delta};d_{\Delta}\right)\right]. (12)

Further details are provided in Appendix D.2, including implementation and optimization specifics.

4.4  Global Transition Anchor

While LT-Filter emphasizes fine-grained local regions with prominent state changes, relying only on the selected top-KK regions risks losing the coarse global context of the overall transition. To preserve global consistency, we introduce the Global Transition Anchor (GT-Anchor) as a coarse transition-level regularization, thereby complementing local selectivity with a scene-level constraint on overall transition direction.

Specifically, we aggregate the dense visual features 𝐕t\mathbf{V}_{t} and 𝐕¯t+H\bar{\mathbf{V}}_{t+H} into KK coarse tokens via adaptive pooling, and construct a global transition anchor that summarizes the overall state evolution direction:

𝐆t=PoolK⁡(𝐕¯t+H)−PoolK⁡(𝐕t)∈ℝK×dv.\mathbf{G}_{t}=\operatorname{Pool}_{K}(\bar{\mathbf{V}}_{t+H})-\operatorname{Pool}_{K}(\mathbf{V}_{t})\in\mathbb{R}^{K\times d_{v}}. (13)

The resulting 𝐆t\mathbf{G}_{t} provides a coarse reference for the transition direction by summarizing large-scale changes across the pooled current and future representations. Meanwhile, the predicted compact Delta Δ^t\hat{\Delta}_{t} is projected back to the high-dimensional visual feature space using an up-projection module g↑g_{\uparrow}:

𝐃^t=g↑​(Δ^t)∈ℝK×dv.\hat{\mathbf{D}}_{t}=g_{\uparrow}(\hat{\Delta}_{t})\in\mathbb{R}^{K\times d_{v}}. (14)

The GT-Anchor objective matches the projected transition tokens with the global transition anchor using the set distance defined in Equation (11) to enforce global consistency across transition representations:

ℒGTA=𝔼τ,ϵΔ​[𝒟set​(𝐃^t,𝐆t,dv)].\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{GTA}}=\mathbb{E}_{\tau,\epsilon_{\Delta}}\left[\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{set}}\left(\hat{\mathbf{D}}_{t},\mathbf{G}_{t};d_{v}\right)\right]. (15)

Importantly, GT-Anchor does not require reconstructing the full future state. Instead, it anchors the compact Delta to the coarse direction of future state transitions, which complements LT-Filter by providing a better balance between expressive capacity and structured transition regularization.

4.5  Delta-Driven Action Refinement

Delta-Seeded Action Flow (DSAF).

Given the predicted Δ^t\hat{\Delta}_{t}, DDAR guides action denoising through two complementary branches: a Delta-induced noise bias and a Delta prefix token. We first aggregate the Delta tokens into a global transition context and map it to an action-space bias:

Δ¯t=1K​∑k=1KΔ^t,k,𝐛t=qb​(Δ¯t)∈ℝH×da.\bar{\Delta}_{t}=\frac{1}{K}\sum_{k=1}^{K}\hat{\Delta}_{t,k},\quad\mathbf{b}_{t}=q_{b}(\bar{\Delta}_{t})\in\mathbb{R}^{H\times d_{a}}. (16)

Instead of standard Gaussian noise, we shift the initial action noise ϵA∼𝒩⁡(0,I)\epsilon_{A}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I) with this Delta-induced bias and construct the action flow path, thereby introducing transition-aware structure at initialization:

ϵA′=ϵA+γ​𝐛t,𝐀τ=τ​ϵA′+(1−τ)​𝐀t,\epsilon_{A}^{\prime}=\epsilon_{A}+\gamma\mathbf{b}_{t},\quad\mathbf{A}_{\tau}=\tau\epsilon_{A}^{\prime}+(1-\tau)\mathbf{A}_{t}, (17)

where γ\gamma is a learnable scalar controlling the bias strength. This path yields the target action velocity 𝐮τA=ϵA′−𝐀t\mathbf{u}_{\tau}^{A}=\epsilon_{A}^{\prime}-\mathbf{A}_{t}. In the second branch, Δ¯t\bar{\Delta}_{t} is projected into a Delta prefix token and prepended to the action tokens during denoising. The Action Expert fϕAf_{\phi}^{A} then predicts the action velocity from the multimodal context, the action flow state, and the prepended Delta context token under this conditioned denoising formulation:

𝐮^τA=fϕA​(𝐀τ,τ,𝐡t,Δ¯t).\hat{\mathbf{u}}_{\tau}^{A}=f_{\phi}^{A}(\mathbf{A}_{\tau},\tau,\mathbf{h}_{t},\bar{\Delta}_{t}). (18)

The action generation objective is defined as an MSE loss:

ℒact=𝔼τ,ϵA​[‖𝐮^τA−𝐮τA‖22].\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{act}}=\mathbb{E}_{\tau,\epsilon_{A}}\left[\|\hat{\mathbf{u}}_{\tau}^{A}-\mathbf{u}_{\tau}^{A}\|_{2}^{2}\right]. (19)

In this way, Delta is not only predicted as an auxiliary transition variable, but also injected into the action flow as a physically grounded prior during downstream action generation and iterative denoising.

Delta-to-Action Manifold Grounding (DAMG).

To ensure that Delta captures action-relevant transitions rather than purely visual changes, we align Delta tokens with action tokens in a shared contrastive space to encourage consistent cross-modal action grounding. We treat the HH ground-truth actions {at+h}h=0H−1\{a_{t+h}\}_{h=0}^{H-1} in the action chunk as positive samples, and randomly sample NN actions from non-overlapping temporal regions of the same trajectory as negative samples. The Delta and action tokens are projected as:

𝐳kΔ=Norm⁡(qΔ​(Δ^t,k)),𝐳hact=Norm⁡(qact​(at+h)).\small\mathbf{z}_{k}^{\Delta}=\operatorname{Norm}(q_{\Delta}(\hat{\Delta}_{t,k})),~~\mathbf{z}_{h}^{\mathrm{act}}=\operatorname{Norm}(q_{\mathrm{act}}(a_{t+h})). (20)

For each positive action token at+ha_{t+h}, we compute its similarity to all Delta tokens using soft token pooling:

sh+=τΔ​log​∑k=1Kexp⁡(⟨𝐳kΔ,𝐳hact⟩τΔ).\small s_{h}^{+}=\tau_{\Delta}\log\sum_{k=1}^{K}\exp\left(\frac{\langle\mathbf{z}_{k}^{\Delta},\mathbf{z}_{h}^{\mathrm{act}}\rangle}{\tau_{\Delta}}\right). (21)

where τΔ\tau_{\Delta} is the pooling temperature controlling soft token aggregation. For the negative actions, we compute their similarities sn−s_{n}^{-} to the Delta set in the same way and optimize an InfoNCE objective:

ℒDDAR=−1H∑h=0H−1logexp⁡(sh+/τc)exp⁡(sh+/τc)+∑n=1Nexp⁡(sn−/τc),\small\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{DDAR}}=-\frac{1}{H}\sum_{h=0}^{H-1}\log\frac{\exp(s_{h}^{+}/\tau_{c})}{\exp(s_{h}^{+}/\tau_{c})+\sum_{n=1}^{N}\exp(s_{n}^{-}/\tau_{c})}, (22)

where τc\tau_{c} is the contrastive temperature controlling positive-negative separation. This alignment grounds Delta in the action manifold, encouraging it to be not only visually predictive but also action-executable.

5  Training Strategy

5.1  Training Objective

Following V-JEPA 2 [2], VLDA employs an online encoder EonE_{\mathrm{on}} for current observations and an EMA teacher EemaE_{\mathrm{ema}} for future observations. Specifically, EonE_{\mathrm{on}} is optimized by gradients, whereas EemaE_{\mathrm{ema}} is updated solely through exponential moving average (see Appendix D.1). This asymmetric design prevents the Delta target from being constructed between two rapidly changing feature spaces, thereby providing stable supervision for future-transition modeling.

VLDA is optimized in two stages to progressively establish transition modeling and action generation. In the first stage (transition pre-training), we learn the transition interface with the Local Transition Filter and Global Transition Anchor objectives, while keeping the action branch frozen:

ℒ(1)=ℒLTF+ℒGTA.\mathcal{L}^{(1)}=\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{LTF}}+\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{GTA}}. (23)

In the second stage, we jointly optimize transition modeling, action generation, and Delta–action alignment:

ℒ(2)=ℒact+λ(1)​ℒ(1)+λDDAR​ℒDDAR.\mathcal{L}^{(2)}=\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{act}}+\lambda_{(1)}\mathcal{L}^{(1)}+\lambda_{\mathrm{DDAR}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{DDAR}}. (24)

5.2  Training Framework

We implement and train VLDA within LoongForge11 1 https://baidu-baige.github.io/LoongForge/ [46], an open-source training framework for large-scale foundation and embodied models. Its PyTorch-native embodied-model subsystem provides modular model, data, and trainer abstractions, supporting distributed training with DDP, ZeRO-1, FSDP, and HSDP. Together with flexible component-wise parameter freezing, checkpoint management, and experiment logging, this infrastructure facilitates the staged optimization of VLDA’s VLM backbone, World Expert, Action Expert, and transition modules. Building upon these capabilities, we implement VLDA-specific Delta target construction, LT-Filter and GT-Anchor objectives, Delta–action alignment, and Delta-driven action refinement, integrating transition learning and action generation within a unified training pipeline.

During inference, VLDA first samples Δ^t\hat{\Delta}_{t} with the World Expert and then uses it as a structured transition prior to guide action denoising via the Action Expert. This inference procedure preserves the understanding–transition–execution decomposition, allowing the predicted Delta to mediate between multimodal task understanding and executable action generation without requiring access to future observations.

6  Experiments

6.1  Experimental Setup

Simulation Benchmarks. We evaluate VLDA on three simulation benchmarks: LIBERO [36], LIBERO-plus [13], and RoboTwin 2.0 [8], covering task generalization, robustness, and cross-distribution generalization. For RoboTwin 2.0, we train on the easy (clean) setting and evaluate on the hard (random) setting. For LIBERO-plus, we directly evaluate the model trained on standard LIBERO in a zero-shot manner. Detailed benchmark descriptions are provided in Appendix A.1.

Real-World Settings.

We evaluate VLDA and two strong baselines on four long-horizon tasks using the GALAXEA R1 Lite [15] and AgileX Cobot Magic [14] platforms. We collect 100, 125, 125, and 150 human-teleoperated demonstrations for the four tasks, respectively, and conduct 25 evaluation trials per task and platform. Detailed settings are provided in Appendix A.2.

Implementation Details.

All experiments are conducted on 8×\times NVIDIA A800-SXM4 (80 GB) GPUs, while real-world inference is performed on a single 32 GB consumer GPU. Further model and training details are provided in Appendix A.3.

6.2  Simulation Results and Analysis

Performance on LIBERO. As shown in Tab. 4, VLDA achieves the best overall performance on LIBERO [36], with an average success rate of 98.5%. By explicitly capturing task-relevant transition cues for action generation while suppressing static and action-irrelevant visual information, its compact actionable Delta consistently improves over the π0.5\pi_{0.5} backbone across Spatial (+1.0), Object (+1.4), Goal (+1.4), and Long (+2.8), while surpassing other recent methods to establish a new state of the art.

Performance on LIBERO-plus.

As shown in Tab. 1, VLDA achieves the best overall zero-shot generalization on LIBERO-Plus [13], with an average success rate of 84.5%, outperforming the π0.5\pi_{0.5} backbone (+10.9) and the strongest baseline, GuidedVLA (+9.1). On the more challenging Long suite, the gains increase to 13.4 and 12.1 points. These results demonstrate that actionable Delta modeling enhances execution consistency and robustness under distribution shifts by focusing on task-relevant transitions.

Performance on RoboTwin 2.0.

As shown in Tab. 2, VLDA achieves a 62.9% average success rate under zero-shot hard evaluation, outperforming the π0.5\pi_{0.5} backbone by 20.2 points and ranking first across all 10 tasks. The gains are particularly pronounced on complex state-transition tasks, including Put Bottles Dustbin (+46), Stacking Three (+30), Place Dual Shoes (+27), and Open Microwave (+27), demonstrating improved robustness to layout, illumination, and appearance shifts through task-relevant Delta modeling.

6.3  Real-world Experimental Analysis

Quantitative Results.

As shown in Tab. 3, VLDA achieves the best real-world performance at 73.0%, outperforming π0.5\pi_{0.5} by 17.0 points. Across four tasks, VLDA maintains higher success rates at later stages, demonstrating stronger long-horizon consistency in spatial alignment, tool use, dynamic manipulation, and bimanual coordination. Basket Relocation further tests spatial generalization using randomized mat positions during data collection and OOD target locations at evaluation. While both baselines degrade sharply at the final placement stage, VLDA retains 72% success (+24), showing robust adaptation to unseen layouts.

Qualitative Visualization.

Fig. 3 shows executions across four real-world tasks. The current-to-future transitions correspond to manipulation actions, including precise placement, tool-mediated transfer, dynamic interception, and bimanual transport. In Basket Relocation, VLDA adapts to the configuration and two OOD mat locations with horizontal and vertical displacements. These results demonstrate that actionable Delta captures manipulation-relevant local changes while preserving the global direction of the transition.

6.4  Ablation Study

Ablation of the Transition Paradigm.

As shown in Tab. 4, we examine transition representation and training strategy. 1) Replacing Delta modeling with Full-Future Prediction reduces performance from 98.5% to 97.8%, showing that state-change modeling is a more effective action interface than full-future prediction. 2) Jointly optimizing modules from the outset reduces performance to 97.3%. These results validate compact Delta modeling and staged optimization for establishing a stable, action-oriented transition interface. Details are provided in Appendix B.2.

Ablation on LT-Filter and GT-Anchor.

As shown in Tab. 5, both modules improve performance in simulation and real-world settings, with their combination achieving the best results throughout. LT-Filter improves performance by suppressing static and action-irrelevant content, while GT-Anchor provides complementary global transition guidance. Their clear gain on Basket Relocation further confirms that local transition selectivity and global relocation consistency are both critical for adapting to varying layouts.

Ablation on Delta-Seeded Action Flow.

As shown in Tab. 4, removing DSAF, including both the Delta-induced noise bias and Delta prefix token, decreases the average success rate from 98.5% to 97.2%. This indicates that using the predicted Delta to seed and condition the action flow enables the Action Expert to better exploit the learned transition prior. More detailed ablations are provided in Appendix B.2.

Ablation on Delta-to-Action Manifold Grounding.

As shown in Tab. 6, Manifold Grounding consistently improves performance on standard LIBERO, with its benefits becoming more pronounced under LIBERO-plus perturbations that alter camera, lighting, background, and noise while preserving task semantics. The gains are especially substantial under lighting (+6.3) and background (+3.7) shifts, indicating that Manifold Grounding steers Delta toward action-relevant transitions while suppressing action-irrelevant visual variations.

6.5  Visualizing Delta Supervision

As shown in Fig. 4, the first three columns present the current observation, future observation, and their dense feature Delta (future minus current), where higher-intensity colors indicate changes. The subsequent columns show that LT-Filter selects sparse manipulation-centric local changes around the target object and interaction regions, while GT-Anchor preserves a coarse scene-level summary of the future transition. Together, they provide complementary local selectivity and global consistency for Delta learning. More visualizations and analyses are provided in Appendix C.2.

7  Conclusion

We propose Vision-Language-Delta-Action (VLDA), which models compact actionable transitions instead of direct actions or complete future states. LT-Filter captures manipulation-relevant changes; GT-Anchor preserves global transition consistency; DDAR grounds Delta and guides action refinement. Experiments demonstrate improved long-horizon consistency, robustness, and spatial generalization, validating actionable Delta as an effective interface between vision-language understanding and action execution.

Appendix A Experimental Details

A.1  Simulation Benchmarks

LIBERO.

LIBERO [36] is a language-conditioned robotic manipulation benchmark designed to evaluate the transfer of declarative and procedural knowledge across tasks. We adopt the four commonly used evaluation suites: Spatial, Object, Goal, and Long, each containing 10 tasks. The Spatial suite requires distinguishing objects according to their relative positions under otherwise similar scene configurations. The Object suite varies the target object while retaining comparable manipulation behaviors and scene layouts. The Goal suite uses similar objects and spatial configurations but changes the desired task goal, thereby emphasizing the transfer of motion and behavioral knowledge. The Long suite consists of compositional, multi-stage tasks that require extended temporal reasoning and coordinated execution.

RoboTwin 2.0.

RoboTwin 2.0 [8] is a simulation benchmark designed for generalizable bimanual manipulation. It provides 50 dual-arm tasks involving diverse objects, scene configurations, and coordinated manipulation skills. In addition to clean environments, the benchmark supports domain-randomized evaluation with variations in scene clutter, illumination, background textures, and tabletop height. These variations jointly alter both visual appearance and object geometry, making the benchmark particularly suitable for evaluating whether a policy can preserve bimanual coordination and task execution under substantial distribution shifts. Under our clean-to-randomized protocol, performance therefore reflects the ability to transfer manipulation knowledge beyond the narrow visual and spatial distribution observed during training.

LIBERO-Plus.

LIBERO-Plus [13] extends the original LIBERO environments with controlled perturbations along seven dimensions: object layouts, camera viewpoints, robot initial states, language instructions, lighting conditions, background textures, and sensor noise. It contains 10,030 perturbed task instances organized into five difficulty levels. In contrast to the broad scene randomization used in RoboTwin 2.0, LIBERO-Plus enables a factor-wise diagnosis of model robustness by isolating individual sources of distribution shift, while also supporting evaluation under combined perturbations. Since no LIBERO-Plus-specific adaptation is performed in our experiments, this benchmark measures whether the representations learned from standard LIBERO remain reliable under unseen changes in viewpoint, robot configuration, visual appearance, language, and observation quality.

A.2  Real-world Platforms and Tasks

GALAXEA R1 Lite Platform.

As shown on the left of Fig. 5, the GALAXEA R1 Lite [15] is a 23-DoF mobile bimanual manipulation platform, comprising a wheeled chassis, an articulated torso, and two 6-DoF robotic arms equipped with parallel grippers. The movable base and torso extend the effective workspace of the robot, while platform-level and wrist-mounted cameras provide complementary global and close-range visual observations. We employ this platform to evaluate VLDA under large-workspace and coordinated bimanual manipulation settings.

AgileX Cobot Magic Platform.

As shown on the right of Fig. 5, the AgileX Cobot Magic platform [14] is a low-cost, open-source bimanual system developed upon Stanford’s Mobile ALOHA project for teleoperated data collection and imitation learning. It integrates a Tracer differential-drive mobile base, two 6-DoF follower arms with parallel-jaw grippers, and RGB-D sensors. During demonstration collection, the follower arms are controlled through a pair of leader arms, while fixed and wrist-mounted RGB cameras provide multi-view observations of the workspace and end-effector interactions. Compared with R1 Lite, ALOHA is operated in a stationary tabletop configuration, emphasizing precise, contact-rich, and tightly coordinated bimanual manipulation.

Real-world Task Details.

We design four long-horizon real-world tasks covering sequential spatial alignment, contact-rich tool use, dynamic target interception, and bimanual object relocation. We collected human-teleoperated demonstrations from individual platforms, with corresponding sample counts of 100, 125, 125, and 150 in order. OpenVLA-OFT, π0.5\pi_{0.5}, and VLDA are trained using the same demonstrations, observations, robot states, and control frequency to ensure a fair comparison.

The language instructions specify only the task objective and necessary semantic order, without exposing low-level actions or evaluation checkpoints. For Basket Relocation, the blue mat is randomly positioned during data collection, and multiple target locations are used during evaluation to assess spatial generalization. Each method is evaluated over 25 physical trials per task and platform. The instructions and progressive checkpoints are summarized in Tab. 7.

Evaluation Protocol.

For each method, task, and platform, we conduct 25 independent physical trials. At the beginning of each trial, task-relevant objects are randomly perturbed within predefined regions while preserving the task semantics. For Conveyor Sorting, the conveyor speed and object release interval are fixed across methods, while the ordering and spacing of target and distractor objects are varied. For Basket Relocation, the blue mat is placed at multiple target locations to evaluate spatial generalization.

Success is recorded at each progressive checkpoint. A trial reaches checkpoint CkC_{k} only if all preceding checkpoints are successfully completed, and complete-task success is defined by the final checkpoint. All results are reported as success rates over 25 trials, while the average success rate is computed from the complete-task success rates across the four tasks.

A.3  Model and Training Details

Architecture and Initialization.

VLDA is implemented on top of π0.5\pi_{0.5}, which consists of a PaliGemma-initialized 2B vision-language backbone and a Gemma-300M Action Expert. We additionally introduce a World Expert with the same transformer architecture and model capacity as the Action Expert. The World Expert is initialized independently from scratch rather than from the pretrained Action Expert.

For visual transition modeling, we adopt the pretrained V-JEPA 2 ViT-g/16 encoder (vjepa2_vit_giant) [2]. The online and teacher encoders are initialized from the encoder and EMA target-encoder branches of the pretrained V-JEPA 2 checkpoint, respectively. Both encoders process the primary-camera image at a resolution of 256×256256\times 256, producing P=256P=256 spatial tokens with dv=1408d_{v}=1408. The primary-view restriction applies only to transition supervision, while the policy backbone continues to process all available camera views at 224×224224\times 224 resolution.

The online encoder is optimized by gradients, whereas the teacher encoder remains gradient-free and is updated exclusively through EMA with momentum m=0.99925m=0.99925. This asymmetric design provides a slowly evolving future-feature target throughout training.

Delta and Projection Modules.

The World Expert predicts K=64K=64 Delta tokens with dΔ=256d_{\Delta}=256. The down-projection g↓g_{\downarrow} and up-projection g↑g_{\uparrow} are implemented as two-layer MLPs with a hidden dimension of 1024. The action-space bias projection qbq_{b} uses the same hidden dimension. Its output layer is zero-initialized, and the unconstrained learnable scale γ\gamma is initialized to 0.010.01.

The mean-pooled Delta is linearly projected into a 1024-dimensional prefix token for the Action Expert. For Delta-action alignment, qΔq_{\Delta} and qactq_{\mathrm{act}} each consist of LayerNorm followed by a linear projection into a shared 256-dimensional contrastive space.

Two-Stage Training.

VLDA is optimized in two stages. During the first stage, termed transition pre-training, we freeze the vision-language backbone and Action Expert, while optimizing the online V-JEPA 2 encoder, World Expert, and transition projection modules. This stage is trained for 10K optimization steps with a global batch size of 48.

The second stage is initialized from the transition-pretraining checkpoint. We unfreeze the vision-language backbone and Action Expert, and jointly optimize all gradient-enabled modules for an additional 60K steps with a global batch size of 128. The World Expert, online encoder, and projection modules remain trainable, while the teacher encoder continues to receive no gradient and is updated solely through EMA.

The LT-Filter and GT-Anchor objectives are equally weighted. We set λ(1)=1\lambda_{(1)}=1 and λDDAR=0.1\lambda_{\mathrm{DDAR}}=0.1 in the second-stage objective. The Delta-token pooling temperature and contrastive temperature are set to τΔ=0.1\tau_{\Delta}=0.1 and τc=0.07\tau_{c}=0.07, respectively.

Both training stages are conducted on a single machine equipped with 8 NVIDIA A800-SXM4 GPUs, each with 80 GB of memory.

Temporal Alignment and Action Sampling.

We use an action horizon of H=10H=10 for the LIBERO-based experiments and H=50H=50 for RoboTwin 2.0. The future observation used to construct transition supervision is aligned with the end of the corresponding action chunk. Near the end of a trajectory, the future index is clipped to the final available frame:

tfuture=min⁡(t+H,Tend).t_{\mathrm{future}}=\min(t+H,T_{\mathrm{end}}). (25)

For Delta-to-Action Manifold Grounding, the ground-truth actions in the current action chunk are treated as positive samples, with the number of positive actions capped at 10. Accordingly, all HH actions are used when H≤10H\leq 10, whereas the first 10 actions are used for longer action chunks. The number of negative actions is set to four times the number of positive actions. These negatives are sampled uniformly without replacement from non-overlapping temporal regions of the same trajectory outside the current action interval.

Inference and Deployment.

During inference, the World Expert generates the Delta-token set using three explicit Euler integration steps. The resulting Delta tokens are mean-pooled and used to construct both the Delta-induced action-noise bias and the Delta prefix token. Conditioned on these two signals, the Action Expert generates the action chunk using ten explicit Euler integration steps.

The two V-JEPA 2 encoders and the modules used exclusively for transition-target construction and Delta-action alignment, including g↓g_{\downarrow}, g↑g_{\uparrow}, qΔq_{\Delta}, and qactq_{\mathrm{act}}, are discarded after training. Deployment therefore requires only the vision-language backbone, World Expert, Delta-to-action conditioning modules, and Action Expert.

Appendix B Extended Quantitative Analyses

B.1  Extended Platform Results

Full Experimental Results on RoboTwin 2.0.

Tab. 8 reports the per-task results over all 50 tasks under the hard randomized setting, with systematic comparisons against ACT [60], Diffusion policy [11], 3D Diffusion policy [55], RDT-1B [38], π0\pi_{0} [4], π0.5\pi_{0.5} [23], TwinVLA (ICLR 2026) [22], BagelVLA [19], and HALO (RA-L 2026) [42]. Although VLDA is trained only on clean demonstrations and directly evaluated under OOD variations without further adaptation, it achieves the highest average success rate of 50.86%, outperforming the strongest baseline, π0.5\pi_{0.5}, by 7.02 percentage points. Compared with these representative imitation-learning, diffusion-based, and VLA baselines, VLDA achieves leading or tied-leading performance across a wide range of tasks involving spatial reasoning, dynamic interaction, long-horizon execution, and bimanual coordination, demonstrating robust generalization to diverse environmental variations.

Real-World Performance on the ALOHA Platform.

As shown in Tab. 9, VLDA remains the strongest method on the ALOHA platform, achieving an average complete-task success rate of 72.0%. This result exceeds π0.5\pi_{0.5} [23] by 18.0 percentage points and OpenVLA-OFT [27] by 55.0 points. These results suggest that VLDA generalizes effectively across sequential assembly, dynamic object interaction, tool-mediated manipulation, and coordinated dual-arm execution.

B.2  Extended Ablation Results

Implementation Details of Transition-Paradigm and Training-Strategy Ablations.

1) Full-Future Prediction. This variant retains the same vision-language backbone, World Expert, output shape (K=64K=64, dΔ=256d_{\Delta}=256), flow formulation, training schedule, DAMG, DSAF, and Action Expert as VLDA. The only difference lies in the supervision target. Instead of constructing current-to-future Delta and applying LT-Filter and GT-Anchor, we encode the future primary-camera observation with the EMA V-JEPA 2 teacher, adaptively pool its 256 patch tokens to 64 tokens, and project them from dv=1408d_{v}=1408 to 256 dimensions. The resulting full-future tokens directly supervise the World Expert using the same xx-prediction and entropy-regularized set-matching objectives. The predicted tokens are then passed through the unchanged World-to-Action pathway.

2) Without Transition Pre-Training. To evaluate the contribution of the two-stage training strategy, this variant removes Stage I and directly performs joint optimization from the same model initialization as VLDA. The vision-language backbone, online V-JEPA 2 encoder, World Expert, Action Expert, and all projection modules are optimized jointly from the beginning using the complete second-stage objective. The EMA teacher remains gradient-free and is updated exclusively through EMA, while the Sinkhorn transport plan remains detached as in the full model. This variant is trained for the same total number of optimization steps as VLDA, with all other architectural settings, loss weights, and inference procedures kept unchanged.

As shown in Tab. 10, VLDA consistently outperforms both variants under distribution shifts. Replacing Delta modeling with full-future prediction reduces the overall success rate from 84.5% to 81.1%, with larger drops under lighting (−6.9-6.9), background (−4.7-4.7), camera (−4.4-4.4), and noise (−3.9-3.9) perturbations. This indicates that directly modeling the complete future representation retains more appearance-dependent and action-irrelevant information, whereas compact Delta provides a more selective transition interface.

Removing transition pre-training further decreases the overall result to 79.4%, with pronounced degradation on the Long suite (−6.1-6.1) and under lighting (−8.3-8.3), background (−6.1-6.1), camera (−5.8-5.8), and noise (−5.1-5.1) shifts. These results suggest that transition pre-training establishes a more stable and robust transition representation before joint action optimization.

Ablation of Delta-Seeded Action Flow.

For Delta-Seeded Action Flow, we conduct a complete ablation of its two Delta-conditioning branches: the Delta-induced noise bias and the Delta prefix token. Specifically, we evaluate three variants: removing both branches, retaining only the noise bias, and retaining only the prefix token. As shown in Tab. 11, both branches contribute to action generation. Using only the Delta-induced noise bias improves the average success rate from 97.2% to 97.9%, while using only the Delta prefix token yields 97.6%. Their combination achieves the best performance of 98.5%, indicating that the noise bias provides a more informative flow initialization, while the prefix token offers complementary transition conditioning throughout denoising.

Ablation of Delta-to-Action Manifold Grounding.

Tab. 14 reports the complete results. Manifold Grounding is applied only during training to align Delta with the current action chunk, introducing no additional inference cost. It yields a modest 0.3-point gain on the nearly saturated LIBERO benchmark, but improves LIBERO-plus by 2.5 points on average, with larger gains under lighting (+6.3), background (+3.7), camera (+2.9), and noise (+2.5) perturbations. Since negative actions are sampled from other temporal regions of the same trajectory, they share the task and scene semantics but correspond to different execution stages. The objective therefore encourages Delta to encode transition cues specific to the current action phase, reducing its reliance on visually variable yet action-irrelevant information.

Ablation of Delta-Induced Noise Bias.

Beyond the branch-wise ablation above, we further investigate how Delta should be incorporated into action-flow initialization. To isolate the noise-bias design, all variants retain the Delta prefix token and differ only in how the initial action source is constructed. We compare the standard Gaussian source without noise shifting, direct injection of the complete Delta-token set, and the proposed mean-pooled action-space bias.

For direct injection, we preserve all Delta tokens and transform them into the shape of the action chunk. Given Δ^t∈ℝK×dΔ\hat{\Delta}_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{K\times d_{\Delta}}, we first project each Delta token into the action dimension:

Qt=qdim​(Δ^t)∈ℝK×da,Q_{t}=q_{\mathrm{dim}}(\hat{\Delta}_{t})\in\mathbb{R}^{K\times d_{a}}, (26)

where qdim:ℝdΔ→ℝdaq_{\mathrm{dim}}:\mathbb{R}^{d_{\Delta}}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{d_{a}} is applied independently to each token. We then mix the token dimension using a learnable projection Wtok∈ℝH×KW_{\mathrm{tok}}\in\mathbb{R}^{H\times K}:

Δ~tA=Wtok​Qt∈ℝH×da.\widetilde{\Delta}_{t}^{A}=W_{\mathrm{tok}}Q_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{H\times d_{a}}. (27)

The transformed Delta is directly added to the Gaussian action source:

ϵA′=ϵA+γ​Δ~tA,ϵA∼𝒩⁡(𝟎,𝐈).\epsilon_{A}^{\prime}=\epsilon_{A}+\gamma\widetilde{\Delta}_{t}^{A},\qquad\epsilon_{A}\sim\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0},\mathbf{I}). (28)

By contrast, the proposed bias first aggregates Delta into the global transition representation Δ¯t\bar{\Delta}_{t} and predicts the action-space bias qb​(Δ¯t)∈ℝH×daq_{b}(\bar{\Delta}_{t})\in\mathbb{R}^{H\times d_{a}}, as defined in the main paper. For the no-shift variant, we simply use ϵA′=ϵA\epsilon_{A}^{\prime}=\epsilon_{A}, following the original action-flow initialization of π0.5\pi_{0.5}.

As shown in Tab. 12, direct Delta injection improves the average success rate from 97.6% to 98.0%, confirming that transition-informed flow initialization facilitates action denoising. The proposed bias further improves performance to 98.5%. Since Delta is learned as an unordered token set, directly projecting all tokens into ordered action positions introduces an additional token-mixing burden. Mean pooling instead provides a permutation-invariant transition summary, which can be adaptively mapped into a more stable and effective action-space bias.

Ablation of Transition-Token Selection.

We examine whether LT-Filter benefits from selecting salient transition regions rather than merely reducing the token number. We compare uniformly sampled Random-KK, adaptive Spatial pooling, and the proposed Top-KK based on ℓ2\ell_{2} transition magnitudes. As shown in Tab. 13, Top-KK outperforms Random-KK and spatial pooling by 1.1 and 0.6 points, respectively. This confirms that explicitly retaining regions with salient changes is more effective than random selection or spatial compression.

Ablation of Set-Matching Objectives.

We compare three objectives for supervising unordered Delta tokens. Point-wise MSE assumes index-wise correspondence, Chamfer distance uses bidirectional nearest-neighbor matching, and entropy-regularized OT performs soft balanced matching. Point-wise MSE and Chamfer distance achieve average success rates of 97.2% and 97.8%, respectively, while OT reaches 98.5%. This demonstrates that soft balanced matching provides more effective supervision than fixed correspondence or independent nearest-neighbor assignments.

Ablation of the Number of Delta Tokens.

We evaluate K∈{16,36,64,100}K\in\{16,36,64,100\} while retaining Top-KK selection and entropy-regularized OT. Increasing KK from 16 to 36 and 64 improves the average success rate from 97.7% to 98.1% and 98.5%, respectively, as more relevant local transitions are preserved. Increasing KK to 100 provides no further average improvement while incurring additional computation. We therefore use K=64K=64 as the default, balancing transition coverage and computational efficiency.
