C.1  Extended Real-World Task Execution Visualization

Execution Visualizations on the GALAXEA R1 Lite Platform.

Fig. 6 presents representative execution trajectories of VLDA on the four long-horizon real-world tasks, together with two OOD spatial configurations of Basket Relocation. Frames are arranged chronologically from left to right, and the colored labels indicate the cumulative evaluation checkpoints defined in Tab. 7. These visualizations demonstrate that VLDA maintains consistent task progress across sequential interaction stages rather than relying on isolated observation-to-action mappings.

  • •

    For Ring Stacking, VLDA first identifies and places the yellow ring around the peg, and subsequently stacks the purple ring above it, successfully preserving the semantic order specified by the instruction.

  • •

    In Conveyor Sorting, the policy intercepts the moving cup and bun in sequence, places the cup upright on the plate, and avoids selecting distractor objects. This task requires both dynamic target tracking and instruction-conditioned object selection.

  • •

    For Table Sweeping, VLDA progressively sweeps the two paper balls into the dustpan, lifts the dustpan while preserving its contents, and finally empties both balls onto the plate. The successful execution illustrates robust contact-rich tool use and consistent maintenance of intermediate task states.

  • •

    Basket Relocation further evaluates long-horizon bimanual coordination and spatial generalization. VLDA sequentially places both toys into the basket, establishes a stable bimanual grasp, and relocates the basket onto the blue mat without dropping either object. Beyond the standard configuration, the bottom two rows visualize OOD settings in which the blue mat is displaced horizontally or vertically relative to the basket. Despite these spatial shifts, VLDA adapts the transport trajectory and completes all checkpoints, indicating that the learned Delta captures the task-relevant transition toward the target region rather than overfitting to fixed absolute layouts.

Execution Visualizations on the AgileX Cobot Magic Platform.

Fig. 7 presents representative VLDA execution trajectories for the four long-horizon tasks on the AgileX Cobot Magic platform, including two OOD spatial configurations of Basket Relocation. Frames proceed chronologically from left to right, with colored labels denoting the cumulative checkpoints in Tab. 7. Across sequential ring stacking, dynamic conveyor sorting, contact-rich table sweeping, and coordinated basket relocation, VLDA consistently completes the required interaction stages while preserving task order and intermediate states. Its successful adaptation to horizontal and vertical displacements of the blue mat further demonstrates robust spatial generalization beyond the training layouts.

C.2  Extended Delta Supervision Visualization

Fig. 8 provides additional visualizations of the Delta supervision on LIBERO (left) and RoboTwin 2.0 (right). For each example, the five columns show the current observation, future observation, dense transition, LT-Filter target, and GT-Anchor target, respectively. The dense transition is computed from the feature difference between the future and current observations, with higher-intensity regions indicating stronger temporal changes.

LT-Filter converts these dense differences into sparse, manipulation-centric targets. Across both benchmarks, the selected patches consistently concentrate around task-relevant objects, end-effectors, contact points, and regions undergoing physical state changes, while suppressing static backgrounds and unrelated scene content. This behavior indicates that LT-Filter isolates the local transition evidence most directly associated with the action being executed. GT-Anchor aggregates future information into a coarse scene-level representation. Its lower-resolution targets preserve the overall spatial direction and structural evolution of the scene, complementing the fine-grained selectivity of LT-Filter. LT-Filter and GT-Anchor enable Delta to retain sparse action-relevant changes while remaining globally aligned with future state evolution, thereby providing a compact and robust transition representation for subsequent action generation.

Appendix D Discussion

D.1  Collapse Mitigation in Transition Representation Learning

In this section, we explain the asymmetric encoder design used for transition representation learning. VLDA employs an online encoder and an EMA teacher encoder to stabilize transition supervision and reduce the risk of representation collapse. Let EψE_{\psi} and Eψ¯E_{\bar{\psi}} denote the online and EMA teacher encoders, respectively. The online encoder is optimized by gradients, whereas the EMA teacher is updated exclusively through exponential moving average:

ψ¯r=m​ψ¯r−1+(1−m)​ψr,m∈[0,1).\bar{\psi}_{r}=m\bar{\psi}_{r-1}+(1-m)\psi_{r},\qquad m\in[0,1). (29)

This design follows the asymmetric optimization principle of V-JEPA 2 [2] and provides a slowly evolving reference for current-to-future transition learning.

Asymmetric Gradient Flow.

The current and future primary-view representations are computed as

𝐕t=Eψ​(Itpri),𝐕¯t+H=sg⁡(Eψ¯​(It+Hpri)),\mathbf{V}_{t}=E_{\psi}(I_{t}^{\mathrm{pri}}),\qquad\bar{\mathbf{V}}_{t+H}=\operatorname{sg}\left(E_{\bar{\psi}}(I_{t+H}^{\mathrm{pri}})\right), (30)

where sg⁡(⋅)\operatorname{sg}(\cdot) denotes stop-gradient. Their dense transition is

𝐃t=𝐕¯t+H−𝐕t.\mathbf{D}_{t}=\bar{\mathbf{V}}_{t+H}-\mathbf{V}_{t}. (31)

The compact Delta target is then constructed as

𝒦t\displaystyle\mathcal{K}_{t} =TopKK⁡({‖𝐃t,i‖2}i=1P),\displaystyle=\operatorname{TopK}_{K}\left(\{\|\mathbf{D}_{t,i}\|_{2}\}_{i=1}^{P}\right), (32)
Δt⋆\displaystyle\Delta_{t}^{\star} =g↓​(𝐃t,𝒦t).\displaystyle=g_{\downarrow}\left(\mathbf{D}_{t,\mathcal{K}_{t}}\right).

Gradients propagate through the selected transition features and the down-projection module, while the discrete Top-KK indices are treated as fixed within each backward pass. No gradient is propagated through the future target branch:

∂Δt⋆∂ψ¯=𝟎,∂Δt⋆∂ψ≠𝟎,∂Δt⋆∂ω↓≠𝟎,\frac{\partial\Delta_{t}^{\star}}{\partial\bar{\psi}}=\mathbf{0},\qquad\frac{\partial\Delta_{t}^{\star}}{\partial\psi}\neq\mathbf{0},\qquad\frac{\partial\Delta_{t}^{\star}}{\partial\omega_{\downarrow}}\neq\mathbf{0}, (33)

where ω↓\omega_{\downarrow} denotes the parameters of g↓g_{\downarrow}. This asymmetric gradient flow keeps the future endpoint fixed within each optimization step and prevents direct gradient-based co-adaptation between the online and teacher branches.

Slowly Evolving Target.

The EMA teacher evolves substantially more slowly than the online encoder. From the EMA update,

ψ¯r−ψ¯r−1=(1−m)​(ψr−ψ¯r−1),\bar{\psi}_{r}-\bar{\psi}_{r-1}=(1-m)\left(\psi_{r}-\bar{\psi}_{r-1}\right), (34)

and consequently

‖ψ¯r−ψ¯r−1‖=(1−m)​‖ψr−ψ¯r−1‖.\left\|\bar{\psi}_{r}-\bar{\psi}_{r-1}\right\|=(1-m)\left\|\psi_{r}-\bar{\psi}_{r-1}\right\|. (35)

When mm is close to one, only a small fraction of the discrepancy between the online and teacher parameters is incorporated at each iteration.

Assuming that the encoder is locally LEL_{E}-Lipschitz with respect to its parameters, the variation of the future representation satisfies

‖Eψ¯r​(It+Hpri)−Eψ¯r−1​(It+Hpri)‖\displaystyle\left\|E_{\bar{\psi}_{r}}(I_{t+H}^{\mathrm{pri}})-E_{\bar{\psi}_{r-1}}(I_{t+H}^{\mathrm{pri}})\right\| (36)
≤LE​(1−m)​‖ψr−ψ¯r−1‖.\displaystyle\leq L_{E}(1-m)\left\|\psi_{r}-\bar{\psi}_{r-1}\right\|.

The future endpoint therefore evolves smoothly rather than changing synchronously with the online representation.

Complementary Transition Constraints.

During Stage I, GT-Anchor requires the predicted compact Delta to explain the pooled transition in the high-dimensional visual feature space. Under the pretrained and non-degenerate visual feature space, these pooled transition anchors vary across samples and execution stages, thereby discouraging the predicted Delta from collapsing to a sample-independent constant representation. GT-Anchor therefore encourages Delta to preserve sample-dependent transition information.

During Stage II, Delta-to-Action Manifold Grounding further requires Delta to distinguish actions in the current chunk from actions sampled from other temporal regions of the same trajectory. Since these negative actions share the same task, scene, and embodiment context but correspond to different execution stages, the alignment objective encourages Delta to retain phase-specific and action-relevant transition information.

The action-generation loss also propagates through the Delta-induced noise bias and Delta prefix token, providing additional action-dependent supervision to the World Expert and the predicted Delta representation.

Transition Representation Stabilization.

Pretrained initialization, asymmetric gradient flow, and slow EMA updates provide a stable and structured future reference for current-to-future transition learning. GT-Anchor encourages sample-dependent global transition information, while Delta-to-Action Manifold Grounding and the action-generation objective further constrain Delta to encode phase-specific and execution-relevant factors. Together, these complementary visual, temporal, and action-grounded constraints reduce rapid co-adaptation and help maintain an informative and actionable Delta space throughout optimization.

D.2  Entropy-Regularized Transport Matching

The token collections compared in LT-Filter and GT-Anchor are treated as unordered sets. Specifically, LT-Filter matches the predicted and target Delta-velocity tokens, while GT-Anchor matches the projected Delta tokens with the global transition anchors. Point-wise regression would impose an arbitrary index-wise correspondence between these tokens. We therefore employ entropy-regularized optimal transport to construct a permutation-invariant soft matching between the two sets.

Let

𝐗=[𝐱1,…,𝐱K]⊤,𝐘=[𝐲1,…,𝐲K]⊤∈ℝK×d.\mathbf{X}=[\mathbf{x}_{1},\ldots,\mathbf{x}_{K}]^{\top},~~\mathbf{Y}=[\mathbf{y}_{1},\ldots,\mathbf{y}_{K}]^{\top}\in\mathbb{R}^{K\times d}. (37)

We assign uniform mass 𝐚=𝐛=1K​𝟏K\mathbf{a}=\mathbf{b}=\frac{1}{K}\mathbf{1}_{K} and define the balanced transport polytope as

Π(𝐚,𝐛)={𝐓∈ℝ+K×K|𝐓𝟏K=𝐚,𝐓⊤𝟏K=𝐛}.\Pi(\mathbf{a},\mathbf{b})=\left\{\mathbf{T}\in\mathbb{R}_{+}^{K\times K}\ \middle|\ \mathbf{T}\mathbf{1}_{K}=\mathbf{a},\,\mathbf{T}^{\top}\mathbf{1}_{K}=\mathbf{b}\right\}. (38)

These constraints ensure that every token in both sets contributes the same total transport mass.

The pairwise token cost is defined as the feature-normalized squared Euclidean distance:

Ci​j=‖𝐱i−𝐲j‖22d.C_{ij}=\frac{\|\mathbf{x}_{i}-\mathbf{y}_{j}\|_{2}^{2}}{d}. (39)

The dimensional normalization enables the same set-matching objective to be applied in both the compact Delta space of dimension dΔd_{\Delta} and the visual feature space of dimension dvd_{v}.

To improve numerical stability when estimating the transport plan, we normalize the cost matrix independently for each sample:

s=max⁡(sg⁡[1K2​∑i,jCi​j],10−6),C¯i​j=Ci​js,s=\max\left(\operatorname{sg}\left[\frac{1}{K^{2}}\sum_{i,j}C_{ij}\right],10^{-6}\right),~~\bar{C}_{ij}=\frac{C_{ij}}{s}, (40)

where sg⁡(⋅)\operatorname{sg}(\cdot) denotes stop-gradient. The normalized cost 𝐂¯\bar{\mathbf{C}} is used only to estimate the transport plan, whereas the final set-matching loss is evaluated using the original cost matrix 𝐂\mathbf{C}.

The entropy-regularized transport plan is defined as

𝐓η⋆=arg⁡min𝐓∈Π⁡(𝐚,𝐛)⁡[⟨𝐓,𝐂¯⟩+η​∑i,jTi​j​log⁡Ti​j],\mathbf{T}_{\eta}^{\star}=\arg\min_{\mathbf{T}\in\Pi(\mathbf{a},\mathbf{b})}\left[\langle\mathbf{T},\bar{\mathbf{C}}\rangle+\eta\sum_{i,j}T_{ij}\log T_{ij}\right], (41)

where ⟨𝐓,𝐂¯⟩=∑i,jTi​j​C¯i​j\langle\mathbf{T},\bar{\mathbf{C}}\rangle=\sum_{i,j}T_{ij}\bar{C}_{ij}, η>0\eta>0 controls the softness of the correspondence, and 0​log⁡0=00\log 0=0. A smaller value of η\eta produces a sharper correspondence, whereas a larger value distributes the transport mass over more token pairs.

We solve Equation (41) using log-domain Sinkhorn iterations. Let

Li​j=−C¯i​jη.L_{ij}=-\frac{\bar{C}_{ij}}{\eta}. (42)

Starting from zero log-scaling vectors 𝐩\mathbf{p} and 𝐪\mathbf{q}, we alternately update

pi\displaystyle p_{i} ←log⁡ai−LSEj⁡(Li​j+qj),\displaystyle\leftarrow\log a_{i}-\operatorname{LSE}_{j}\left(L_{ij}+q_{j}\right), (43)
qj\displaystyle q_{j} ←log⁡bj−LSEi⁡(Li​j+pi),\displaystyle\leftarrow\log b_{j}-\operatorname{LSE}_{i}\left(L_{ij}+p_{i}\right),

where LSE\operatorname{LSE} denotes the log-sum-exp operation. The resulting transport plan is

Tη,i​j⋆=exp⁡(Li​j+pi+qj).T_{\eta,ij}^{\star}=\exp\left(L_{ij}+p_{i}+q_{j}\right). (44)

We use 50 Sinkhorn iterations and set η=0.05\eta=0.05 in all experiments.

The transport plan is used only to determine the soft correspondence. We therefore stop gradients through the Sinkhorn solver:

𝐓~η=sg⁡(𝐓η⋆).\widetilde{\mathbf{T}}_{\eta}=\operatorname{sg}\left(\mathbf{T}_{\eta}^{\star}\right). (45)

The set-matching loss used in the main paper is implemented as

𝒟set​(𝐗,𝐘,d)=⟨𝐓~η,𝐂⟩=∑i,jT~η,i​j​Ci​j.\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{set}}(\mathbf{X},\mathbf{Y};d)=\left\langle\widetilde{\mathbf{T}}_{\eta},\mathbf{C}\right\rangle=\sum_{i,j}\widetilde{T}_{\eta,ij}C_{ij}. (46)

Thus, entropy regularization influences optimization through the soft correspondence encoded by 𝐓~η\widetilde{\mathbf{T}}_{\eta}, while the entropy term itself is not added to the final scalar training loss. Gradients propagate through the original pairwise costs to the token features without back-propagating through the Sinkhorn iterations.

Finally, let 𝐏\mathbf{P} and 𝐑\mathbf{R} be arbitrary permutation matrices applied independently to the two token sets. The corresponding cost and transport matrices are permuted as 𝐏𝐂𝐑⊤\mathbf{P}\mathbf{C}\mathbf{R}^{\top} and 𝐏𝐓η⋆​𝐑⊤\mathbf{P}\mathbf{T}_{\eta}^{\star}\mathbf{R}^{\top}, respectively. Consequently,

𝒟set​(𝐏𝐗,𝐑𝐘,d)=𝒟set​(𝐗,𝐘,d).\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{set}}(\mathbf{P}\mathbf{X},\mathbf{R}\mathbf{Y};d)=\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{set}}(\mathbf{X},\mathbf{Y};d). (47)

The objective therefore requires neither fixed token identities nor a predefined ordering of the Delta or transition-anchor tokens.

D.3  Supplementary Details on Motivation

This section further explains the design considerations behind actionable Delta modeling, including the choice of transition targets, the complementary supervision objectives, and the role of Delta in action generation.

Why an Actionable Transition Interface?

Direct observation-to-action policies must implicitly infer the desired physical change and translate it into motor commands within a single representation. Complete future-state prediction introduces temporal structure, but its target contains both the state information already present in the current observation and the comparatively sparse changes caused by manipulation. Consequently, a large portion of its learning capacity may be devoted to reconstructing static objects, background appearance, and other information that does not determine the next action.

Delta provides an intermediate alternative between these two formulations. Rather than reproducing the complete future state or mapping semantic observations directly to actions, it explicitly represents the transition between the current and future states. Feature differencing suppresses much of the shared appearance content, while the compact token space further limits residual redundancy. Delta is therefore not intended to reconstruct every future detail; it serves as a control-oriented interface that conveys the physical transition most useful for subsequent action generation.

Why Horizon-Aligned Future Supervision?

The future observation at t+Ht+H is aligned with the action chunk 𝐀t=[at,…,at+H−1]\mathbf{A}_{t}=[a_{t},\ldots,a_{t+H-1}]. It records the state reached after executing the actions covered by the current prediction horizon, making the current-to-future difference a natural supervision signal for the physical effect of that chunk. A substantially shorter transition would describe only an early fraction of the predicted motion, whereas a substantially longer transition could include state changes beyond the temporal scope of the current action chunk.

Why Combine Local and Global Transition Supervision?

A useful transition representation must be selective without becoming myopic. LT-Filter addresses selectivity by retaining regions with large feature-transition magnitudes. This suppresses the many spatial tokens whose current and future representations remain nearly unchanged and emphasizes candidate interaction regions. However, magnitude-based selection alone can overemphasize isolated local changes or discard distributed transitions, such as the overall displacement of a large object.

GT-Anchor provides the complementary constraint. By pooling before computing the transition, it retains a coarse summary of the overall state evolution without requiring reconstruction of the complete future feature map. LT-Filter can therefore be viewed as preserving high-resolution local evidence, while GT-Anchor preserves low-resolution global consistency. Their combination encourages Delta to capture manipulation-centric details while remaining compatible with the broader direction of future evolution.

Why Ground Delta in the Action Manifold?

Visual transition supervision alone does not guarantee action relevance. Feature differences may also reflect illumination changes, background motion, or object changes that are visually salient but unrelated to the demonstrated behavior. Delta-to-Action Manifold Grounding addresses this ambiguity by comparing every action in the current chunk with the predicted Delta-token set. Actions from the corresponding chunk serve as positives, while actions from non-overlapping regions of the same trajectory serve as negatives.

Sampling negatives from the same trajectory is important because it controls for much of the shared scene, task, and embodiment context. The alignment objective must therefore distinguish the action associated with the current local transition from other individually plausible actions in the same demonstration. As detailed in Appendix D.4, this action-wise InfoNCE objective admits a conditional mutual-information interpretation. It encourages Delta to retain transition factors that are informative about all actions in the current chunk rather than merely encoding visually predictive appearance changes.

Why Two-Stage Optimization?

The World Expert and the Delta pathway are newly introduced components, whereas the VLM and Action Expert inherit strong pretrained representations. If all objectives are optimized jointly from the beginning, the pretrained action pathway can reduce the action loss without consistently relying on the initially unstructured Delta representation. This can weaken the role of Delta as an explicit transition interface.

The first stage therefore optimizes LT-Filter and GT-Anchor before joint action training, allowing the World Expert to establish a stable and future-grounded transition space. The second stage then introduces action generation and Delta–Action alignment, grounding this learned transition space in executable behavior. The observed degradation under one-stage training further supports the benefit of establishing the transition interface before joint action refinement.

D.4  Mathematical Details of Key Equations

In this section, we provide mathematical details for the key objectives in VLDA, including the expert-specific flow parameterizations and the mutual information maximization perspective of Delta-to-Action Manifold Grounding.

Expert-Specific Flow Parameterizations.

The Action and World Experts share the same linear conditional path but use different source distributions. For E∈{A,Δ}E\in\{A,\Delta\}, let

(𝐱0A,𝐳A)\displaystyle(\mathbf{x}_{0}^{A},\mathbf{z}_{A}) =(𝐀t,ϵA+γ​𝐛t),\displaystyle=(\mathbf{A}_{t},\epsilon_{A}+\gamma\mathbf{b}_{t}), (48)
(𝐱0Δ,𝐳Δ)\displaystyle(\mathbf{x}_{0}^{\Delta},\mathbf{z}_{\Delta}) =(Δt⋆,ϵΔ).\displaystyle=(\Delta_{t}^{\star},\epsilon_{\Delta}).

Conditioned on the predicted action-space bias 𝐛t\mathbf{b}_{t}, the corresponding source distributions are

𝐳A∼𝒩⁡(γ​𝐛t,𝐈),𝐳Δ∼𝒩⁡(𝟎,𝐈).\mathbf{z}_{A}\sim\mathcal{N}(\gamma\mathbf{b}_{t},\mathbf{I}),\qquad\mathbf{z}_{\Delta}\sim\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0},\mathbf{I}). (49)

During Stage II, 𝐛t\mathbf{b}_{t} remains differentiable, allowing the action-generation objective to update γ\gamma, qbq_{b}, and the upstream Delta pathway.

Both experts follow the linear conditional path

𝐱τE=(1−τ)​𝐱0E+τ​𝐳E,\mathbf{x}_{\tau}^{E}=(1-\tau)\mathbf{x}_{0}^{E}+\tau\mathbf{z}_{E}, (50)

which satisfies 𝐱τ=0E=𝐱0E\mathbf{x}_{\tau=0}^{E}=\mathbf{x}_{0}^{E} and 𝐱τ=1E=𝐳E\mathbf{x}_{\tau=1}^{E}=\mathbf{z}_{E}. Its derivative gives the constant conditional velocity

d​𝐱τEd​τ=𝐳E−𝐱0E=𝐮τE.\frac{\mathrm{d}\mathbf{x}_{\tau}^{E}}{\mathrm{d}\tau}=\mathbf{z}_{E}-\mathbf{x}_{0}^{E}=\mathbf{u}_{\tau}^{E}. (51)

The Action Expert directly predicts this velocity. For the World Expert, the Delta path gives, for τ>0\tau>0,

𝐮τΔ=Δτ−Δt⋆τ.\mathbf{u}_{\tau}^{\Delta}=\frac{\Delta_{\tau}-\Delta_{t}^{\star}}{\tau}. (52)

Replacing the clean endpoint with the World-Expert prediction gives

𝐮^τΔ=Δτ−Δ^tτ,𝐮^τΔ−𝐮τΔ=Δt⋆−Δ^tτ.\hat{\mathbf{u}}_{\tau}^{\Delta}=\frac{\Delta_{\tau}-\hat{\Delta}_{t}}{\tau},\qquad\hat{\mathbf{u}}_{\tau}^{\Delta}-\mathbf{u}_{\tau}^{\Delta}=\frac{\Delta_{t}^{\star}-\hat{\Delta}_{t}}{\tau}. (53)

For numerical stability, the World-Expert flow time is sampled as

τ=0.999​ξ,ξ∼Beta⁡(1.5,1.0).\tau=0.999\xi,\qquad\xi\sim\operatorname{Beta}(1.5,1.0). (54)

When converting xx-predictions into velocities, we use

τ~=max⁡(τ,τmin),τmin=0.05,\widetilde{\tau}=\max(\tau,\tau_{\min}),\qquad\tau_{\min}=0.05, (55)

and compute

𝐮τ,stabΔ=Δτ−Δt⋆τ~,𝐮^τ,stabΔ=Δτ−Δ^tτ~.\mathbf{u}_{\tau,\mathrm{stab}}^{\Delta}=\frac{\Delta_{\tau}-\Delta_{t}^{\star}}{\widetilde{\tau}},\qquad\hat{\mathbf{u}}_{\tau,\mathrm{stab}}^{\Delta}=\frac{\Delta_{\tau}-\hat{\Delta}_{t}}{\widetilde{\tau}}. (56)

The same stabilized denominator is used for the target and predicted velocities, and no additional time-dependent loss weighting is applied. This bounds endpoint-error amplification by 1/τmin=201/\tau_{\min}=20. Therefore, the shifted action source modifies the source boundary while preserving the linear conditional path, whereas the World Expert uses a numerically stabilized conversion from xx-prediction to velocity prediction.

Mathematical Properties of Delta-Action Alignment.

We further analyze the Delta-action alignment objective introduced in Section 4.5 of the main paper. Let Δ={Δk}k=1K\Delta=\{\Delta_{k}\}_{k=1}^{K} denote the predicted Delta-token set, and let aa denote an individual action token. For notational simplicity, HH below denotes the number of positive actions used by the alignment objective; in implementation, this number is capped at 10.

The projected and normalized representations are

𝐳kΔ\displaystyle\mathbf{z}_{k}^{\Delta} =Norm⁡(qΔ​(Δk)),\displaystyle=\operatorname{Norm}\left(q_{\Delta}(\Delta_{k})\right), (57)
𝐳act​(a)\displaystyle\mathbf{z}^{\mathrm{act}}(a) =Norm⁡(qact​(a)).\displaystyle=\operatorname{Norm}\left(q_{\mathrm{act}}(a)\right).

Let

ck​(Δ,a)=⟨𝐳kΔ,𝐳act​(a)⟩c_{k}(\Delta,a)=\left\langle\mathbf{z}_{k}^{\Delta},\mathbf{z}^{\mathrm{act}}(a)\right\rangle (58)

denote the similarity between the kk-th Delta token and the action token. The soft token-pooled similarity is

s⁡(Δ,a)=τΔ​log​∑k=1Kexp⁡(ck​(Δ,a)τΔ).s(\Delta,a)=\tau_{\Delta}\log\sum_{k=1}^{K}\exp\left(\frac{c_{k}(\Delta,a)}{\tau_{\Delta}}\right). (59)

Permutation Invariance and Soft Token Assignment.

Because Equation (59) sums over the complete Delta-token set, its value is invariant to any permutation of the Delta tokens. For an arbitrary permutation matrix 𝐏\mathbf{P},

s⁡(𝐏​Δ,a)=s⁡(Δ,a).s(\mathbf{P}\Delta,a)=s(\Delta,a). (60)

Therefore, Delta-action alignment does not require a fixed token identity or predefined token ordering.

Define the token-assignment weights as

αk​(Δ,a)=exp⁡(ck​(Δ,a)/τΔ)∑j=1Kexp⁡(cj​(Δ,a)/τΔ).\alpha_{k}(\Delta,a)=\frac{\exp\left(c_{k}(\Delta,a)/\tau_{\Delta}\right)}{\sum_{j=1}^{K}\exp\left(c_{j}(\Delta,a)/\tau_{\Delta}\right)}. (61)

The derivative of the pooled similarity with respect to each token-action similarity is

∂s⁡(Δ,a)∂ck​(Δ,a)=αk​(Δ,a).\frac{\partial s(\Delta,a)}{\partial c_{k}(\Delta,a)}=\alpha_{k}(\Delta,a). (62)

Thus, the alignment gradient is distributed across Delta tokens according to their compatibility with the action. Highly relevant tokens receive larger gradients, while less relevant tokens contribute less, without requiring a discrete token assignment.

The pooled similarity also satisfies

maxk⁡ck​(Δ,a)≤s⁡(Δ,a)≤maxk⁡ck​(Δ,a)+τΔ​log⁡K.\displaystyle\max_{k}c_{k}(\Delta,a)\leq s(\Delta,a)\leq\max_{k}c_{k}(\Delta,a)+\tau_{\Delta}\log K. (63)

As τΔ→0\tau_{\Delta}\rightarrow 0, the pooled similarity approaches the maximum token-action similarity:

limτΔ→0s⁡(Δ,a)=maxk⁡ck​(Δ,a).\lim_{\tau_{\Delta}\rightarrow 0}s(\Delta,a)=\max_{k}c_{k}(\Delta,a). (64)

Consequently, soft token pooling can be interpreted as a smooth matching between each action token and the most compatible transition tokens. Unlike mean pooling, it preserves token-level selectivity while remaining differentiable and permutation invariant.

Action-Wise Contrastive Optimization.

The contrastive critic is defined as

f⁡(Δ,a)=s⁡(Δ,a)τc.f(\Delta,a)=\frac{s(\Delta,a)}{\tau_{c}}. (65)

For each positive action at+ha_{t+h} and NN negative actions {an−}n=1N\{a_{n}^{-}\}_{n=1}^{N}, the action-wise contrastive loss is

ℓh=−log⁡exp⁡f⁡(Δ,at+h)exp⁡f⁡(Δ,at+h)+∑n=1Nexp⁡f⁡(Δ,an−).\ell_{h}=-\log\frac{\exp f(\Delta,a_{t+h})}{\exp f(\Delta,a_{t+h})+\sum_{n=1}^{N}\exp f(\Delta,a_{n}^{-})}. (66)

Let the positive candidate have index 00, and let a0=at+ha_{0}=a_{t+h} and an=an−a_{n}=a_{n}^{-} for n≥1n\geq 1. Define

πj=exp⁡f⁡(Δ,aj)∑m=0Nexp⁡f⁡(Δ,am).\pi_{j}=\frac{\exp f(\Delta,a_{j})}{\sum_{m=0}^{N}\exp f(\Delta,a_{m})}. (67)

The gradients with respect to the candidate scores are

∂ℓh∂f⁡(Δ,aj)=πj−𝟏[j=0].\frac{\partial\ell_{h}}{\partial f(\Delta,a_{j})}=\pi_{j}-\mathbf{1}[j=0]. (68)

In particular,

∂ℓh∂f⁡(Δ,at+h)=π0−1,∂ℓh∂f⁡(Δ,an−)=πn.\frac{\partial\ell_{h}}{\partial f(\Delta,a_{t+h})}=\pi_{0}-1,\qquad\frac{\partial\ell_{h}}{\partial f(\Delta,a_{n}^{-})}=\pi_{n}. (69)

The objective therefore increases the compatibility between Delta and the current positive action, while decreasing its compatibility with actions from other execution stages. Negatives receiving larger softmax probabilities also receive larger repulsive gradients, providing an implicit emphasis on more confusable action phases.

The complete alignment objective averages over the selected actions in the current chunk:

ℒDDAR=1H​∑h=0H−1𝔼⁡[ℓh].\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{DDAR}}=\frac{1}{H}\sum_{h=0}^{H-1}\mathbb{E}[\ell_{h}]. (70)

Idealized Conditional InfoNCE Interpretation.

We next provide an idealized mutual-information interpretation. Let 𝒞\mathcal{C} denote the task, scene, and embodiment context shared by the positive and negative candidates, excluding their temporal action identity. Suppose that, conditioned on 𝒞\mathcal{C}, the positive action is sampled from

a+∼p⁡(a∣Δ,𝒞),a^{+}\sim p(a\mid\Delta,\mathcal{C}), (71)

whereas the negative actions are independently sampled from

an−​∼i.i.d.​p​(a∣𝒞).a_{n}^{-}\overset{\mathrm{i.i.d.}}{\sim}p(a\mid\mathcal{C}). (72)

The corresponding conditional density ratio is

ρ𝒞​(Δ,a)=p⁡(a∣Δ,𝒞)p⁡(a∣𝒞).\rho_{\mathcal{C}}(\Delta,a)=\frac{p(a\mid\Delta,\mathcal{C})}{p(a\mid\mathcal{C})}. (73)

Consider a candidate set containing one positive and NN negative actions, and let J∈{0,…,N}J\in\{0,\ldots,N\} indicate the index of the positive candidate. Under the idealized sampling process, its posterior is

p(J=j∣Δ,a0:N,𝒞)=ρ𝒞​(Δ,aj)∑m=0Nρ𝒞​(Δ,am).p\left(J=j\mid\Delta,a_{0:N},\mathcal{C}\right)=\frac{\rho_{\mathcal{C}}(\Delta,a_{j})}{\sum_{m=0}^{N}\rho_{\mathcal{C}}(\Delta,a_{m})}. (74)

Accordingly, the optimal contrastive critic has the density-ratio form

f𝒞⋆​(Δ,a)=log⁡p⁡(a∣Δ,𝒞)p⁡(a∣𝒞)+c⁡(Δ,𝒞),f_{\mathcal{C}}^{\star}(\Delta,a)=\log\frac{p(a\mid\Delta,\mathcal{C})}{p(a\mid\mathcal{C})}+c(\Delta,\mathcal{C}), (75)

where c⁡(Δ,𝒞)c(\Delta,\mathcal{C}) does not depend on the action candidate and therefore cancels in the softmax.

Under these assumptions, the standard InfoNCE result implies [48]

I⁡(Δ;at+h∣𝒞)≥log⁡(N+1)−ℒh,I\left(\Delta;a_{t+h}\mid\mathcal{C}\right)\geq\log(N+1)-\mathcal{L}_{h}, (76)

where ℒh=𝔼⁡[ℓh]\mathcal{L}_{h}=\mathbb{E}[\ell_{h}]. Averaging over the selected actions gives

1H​∑h=0H−1I⁡(Δ;at+h∣𝒞)≥log⁡(N+1)−ℒDDAR.\frac{1}{H}\sum_{h=0}^{H-1}I\left(\Delta;a_{t+h}\mid\mathcal{C}\right)\geq\log(N+1)-\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{DDAR}}. (77)

Since each at+ha_{t+h} is a component of the complete action chunk 𝐀t\mathbf{A}_{t}, the data-processing property gives

I⁡(Δ;𝐀t∣𝒞)≥I⁡(Δ;at+h∣𝒞)I\left(\Delta;\mathbf{A}_{t}\mid\mathcal{C}\right)\geq I\left(\Delta;a_{t+h}\mid\mathcal{C}\right) (78)

for every hh. Therefore,

I⁡(Δ;𝐀t∣𝒞)\displaystyle I\left(\Delta;\mathbf{A}_{t}\mid\mathcal{C}\right) ≥max0≤h<H⁡I⁡(Δ;at+h∣𝒞)\displaystyle\geq\max_{0\leq h<H}I\left(\Delta;a_{t+h}\mid\mathcal{C}\right) (79)
≥1H​∑h=0H−1I⁡(Δ;at+h∣𝒞)\displaystyle\geq\frac{1}{H}\sum_{h=0}^{H-1}I\left(\Delta;a_{t+h}\mid\mathcal{C}\right)
≥log⁡(N+1)−ℒDDAR.\displaystyle\geq\log(N+1)-\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{DDAR}}.

Thus, under the idealized conditional negative-sampling assumption, the action-wise alignment objective admits a lower-bound interpretation for the conditional mutual information between Delta and the complete action chunk.

Relation to Practical Negative Sampling.

In practice, negative actions are sampled uniformly without replacement from non-overlapping temporal regions of the same trajectory. This sampling strategy keeps the task, scene, and embodiment context close to that of the positive action while changing the execution stage. It therefore prevents the contrastive task from being solved primarily through task- or scene-level differences.

The practical negatives are not strictly independent samples from an exact population marginal, so the lower bound in Equation (79) should be interpreted under the idealized sampling model above. The implemented loss is more precisely an InfoNCE-based structured contrastive surrogate. Independently of the mutual-information interpretation, however, the permutation invariance in Equation (59), the soft token assignments in Equation (61), and the contrastive gradient in Equation (68) hold exactly for the implemented objective. These properties encourage Delta to retain transition information that distinguishes the current execution phase from other actions within the same task trajectory.

D.5  Limitations and Future Work

While Vision-Language-Delta-Action (VLDA) provides a principled transition interface that improves manipulation performance, robustness, and long-horizon consistency, several limitations remain to be addressed in future work:

Sensitivity to Unrelated Visual Dynamics.

The Local Transition Filter (LT-Filter) selects task-relevant changes based on the feature difference magnitude between current and future observations. Although the rich semantic priors from the V-JEPA 2 encoder significantly suppress pixel-level high-frequency noise, intense background motion (e.g., dynamic screens, moving bystanders) could occasionally pollute the top-KK selection. Future extensions could incorporate manipulation-centric visual grounding or instruction-attentive filters to explicitly isolate robot- and manipulation-centric regions from background clutter.

Fixed Horizon State Transition Modeling.

Currently, VLDA models state transitions over a fixed temporal horizon HH, dictated by the action chunking size. However, complex real-world tasks often involve variable-speed trajectories or multi-rate execution where state transitions naturally span non-uniform temporal spans. Extending the compact Delta interface to hierarchical or adaptively spaced temporal horizons represents a promising avenue for flexible long-horizon execution.

Cross-Embodiment Transition Transfer.

Because the compact Delta representation focuses on physical world state changes rather than robot-specific joint configurations, it holds strong potential as an embodiment-agnostic control interface. Future work will investigate leveraging Delta targets for cross-robot skill transfer, where a transition model learned on one physical arm guides policy execution across diverse robotic platforms with minimal adaptation.
